text.p: Enron Corp., the Houston-based energy giant has agreed to a special meeting with the Oregon Public Utility Commission to discuss its bid to merge with Portland General Corp.

The announcement of the Feb. 14 meeting follows Friday's breakdown of earlier talks with utility commission staff, who objected to Enron's proposal of $12 million in rate cuts to cucstomers over the next four years against a their proposal of $177.6 million.

Phil Nyegaard, administrator of the PUC's financial-analysis division, said the Enron group had voted to accept an offer of a special meeting with three utility commissioners. "We're quite comfortable with where we are now," he said..
Neither Enron spokesman Gary Foster in Houston nor the PUC, which is expected to support its staff recommendations, had comment.

Enron, a $15-billion international gas and electricity producer, wants to merge with Portland General, a $3.2 billion regional firm with a strong base of inexpensive hydroelectric and gas-turbine electricity. Shareholders and directors of both companies have approved the merger, but it still needs the Oregon PUC and Federal Energy Regulatory Commission permission to be complete. The target date for Oregon approval is March 17.
The merger has been closely watched because neighboring California has already begun deregulating its electric utilities to allow open competition among electricity vendors.

Enron has already signed one deal to help arrange supplies for a group of 11 northern California utilities, and is a leading bidder for a similar arrangement with the big Los Angeles Department of Water & Power.

Enron and the PUC disagree on the state's role in the merger. The PUC says Oregon law requires that a merger must bring benefits to customers. Enron disagrees, saying the law only requires that customers not be harmed, and has refused to furnish the PUC with details of specific cost-saving measures it intends to take after the merger.

The PUC staff has proposed that the PUC approve the merger, but with 23 stipulations that prevent Enron from investing Portland General's capital elsewhere, and that give Oregon customers some benefits from plants that they have been paying for in their electric bills.
